hints: Recall that a chiral carbon must be sp3 tetrahedral and bonded to four completely different atoms or groups, so check each benzylic carbon for this.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
Picture yourself sitting with the scheme and testing every carbon. A chiral centre needs four single bonds to four different things. $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups can never be chiral, $\text{C=C}$ carbons can never be chiral, and benzene ring carbons can never be chiral.

Find the two that pass**
In the cyanohydrin, the carbon joined to the ring carries $\text{-OH}$, $\text{-CN}$, $\text{-CH}_{3}$ and the $\text{4-(2-methylpropyl)phenyl}$ group. Four different groups, so it is chiral. In ibuprofen, the carbon joined to the ring carries $\text{-H}$, $\text{-CH}_{3}$, $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and the aryl group. Four different groups, so it is also chiral. The isobutyl side chain carbons, the alkene $\text{C(CO}_{2}\text{H)=CH}_{2}$ carbons and the other quaternary carbons all have two identical $\text{H}$ or $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups or are planar, so they are achiral.

Final answer: Circle the $\text{C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CN)}$ carbon in the cyanohydrin intermediate and the $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)(CO}_{2}\text{H)}$ carbon in ibuprofen. No other displayed carbons are chiral.

hints: Work backwards from the cyanohydrin to H: step 3 adds HCN across a C=O bond, so what carbonyl compound must H have been?

Work forwards from the cyanohydrin to the alkene acid: step 4 and step 5 together must convert -C(OH)(CH3)(CN) into -C(CO2H)=CH2 by hydrolysis of nitrile and loss of water, so consider the two possible orders.
walkthrough:
Deduce H by reversing cyanohydrin formation**
Step 3 turns H into $\text{Ar-C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CN)}$. You know aldehydes and ketones react with $\text{HCN}$ to give cyanohydrins by adding $\text{H}$ to oxygen and $\text{CN}$ to carbon. So just remove $\text{HCN}$: replace $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-CN}$ on that carbon by $\text{=O}$. That leaves $\text{Ar-COCH}_{3}$ with the $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ group still para to it. That is H, a methyl ketone.

Deduce J by tracking hydrolysis plus dehydration**
From the cyanohydrin $\text{Ar-C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CN)}$ to the alkene acid $\text{Ar-C(CO}_{2}\text{H)=CH}_{2}$ you need two changes: $\text{-CN}$ hydrolysed to $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$, and $\text{-OH}$ plus a $\text{H}$ from the $\text{CH}_{3}$ lost as water to form $\text{C=CH}_{2}$. If hydrolysis happens first, J is the hydroxy-acid $\text{Ar-C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CO}_{2}\text{H)}$. If dehydration happens first, J is the unsaturated nitrile $\text{Ar-C(CN)=CH}_{2}$. Either is accepted as J because steps 4 and 5 can be in either order.

Final answer: H is $\text{4-(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COCH}_{3}$ (para-isobutyl phenyl methyl ketone).
J is either J1: $\text{4-(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CO}_{2}\text{H)}$ (hydroxy-acid) or J2: $\text{4-(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-C(CN)=CH}_{2}$ (unsaturated nitrile).

hints: Steps 1 and 2 both add carbon groups to a benzene ring, so think which type of Friedel-Crafts reaction and which catalyst is used for alkyl versus acyl halides.
Step 1 adds a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ group and step 2 adds a $\text{COCH}_{3}$ group para to it, so identify the matching chloroalkane and acyl chloride.
Step 3 forms a cyanohydrin from a ketone, so recall the need for $\text{HCN}$ with a source of $\text{CN}^{-}$ as catalyst.
One of steps 4 or 5 converts $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$, so recall the vigorous aqueous acid hydrolysis conditions for nitriles.
The other of steps 4 or 5 converts an alcohol to an alkene $\text{C=CH}_{2}$, so recall the concentrated acid or hot alumina dehydration conditions.
Step 6 converts $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{CH-CH}_{3}$ to give ibuprofen, so recall the standard alkene hydrogenation reagents.
walkthrough:
Build the alkylbenzene with Friedel-Crafts alkylation**
Benzene to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ is adding an isobutyl group to the ring. That is electrophilic substitution by an alkyl halide. Use $\text{1-chloro-2-methylpropane}$, $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, with the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ and heat to generate the electrophile.

Add the acetyl group with Friedel-Crafts acylation**
Next you go to the para methyl ketone H, $\text{Ar-COCH}_{3}$. Acylation uses an acyl chloride plus $\text{AlCl}_{3}$. So use $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_{3}$ with heat. The isobutyl group is activating and ortho, para directing, and para product is favoured on steric grounds.

Make the cyanohydrin**
Ketone plus hydrogen cyanide gives the cyanohydrin. $\text{HCN}$ alone is very slow, you need cyanide ion as catalyst. So use $\text{HCN} + \text{NaCN}$ (or $\text{KCN}$, or $\text{HCN}$ with a little base or $\text{CN}^{-}$). Keep conditions cold, as this is nucleophilic addition.

Hydrolyse the nitrile and dehydrate the alcohol in either order**
To get from $\text{-C(OH)(CH}_{3}\text{)(CN)}$ to $\text{-C(CO}_{2}\text{H)=CH}_{2}$ you need vigorous acid hydrolysis: aqueous $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$ with heat, which converts $\text{-CN}$ via amide to $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. You also need dehydration of the tertiary alcohol: conc $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ with heat (or conc $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ with heat, or hot $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$). If hydrolysis is step 4 then dehydration is step 5 (via J1 hydroxy-acid). If dehydration is step 4 then hydrolysis is step 5 (via J2 unsaturated nitrile).

Reduce the alkene to the alkane**
The last step is $\text{Ar-C(CO}_{2}\text{H)=CH}_{2}$ to $\text{Ar-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)(CO}_{2}\text{H)}$, simple addition of $\text{H}_{2}$ across $\text{C=C}$. Use $\text{H}_{2}$ with $\text{Ni}$ catalyst (with heat). $\text{Pt}$ or $\text{Pd}$ also work. The benzene ring and carboxylic acid are untouched under these mild conditions.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_{3}$, heat
step 2: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_{3}$, heat
step 3: $\text{HCN} + \text{NaCN}$ (or $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{CN}^{-}$ / trace base)
step 4 and step 5 in either order: $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$, heat / aqueous $\text{HCl}$, heat for hydrolysis; conc $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, heat (or conc $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, heat or $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, heat) for dehydration
step 6: $\text{H}_{2} + \text{Ni}$ (heat, or Pt / Pd catalyst)

hints: Recall the general mechanism name when an electrophile generated by AlCl3 attacks a benzene ring in step 1.
Consider what happens to the carbon carbon double bond in step 6 in terms of gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Name the ring mechanism**
In step 1 benzene uses its pi electrons to attack an electrophile formed from the alkyl chloride and $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, then loses $\text{H}^{+}$ to restore aromaticity. That is the classic electrophilic substitution pattern, here specifically alkylation.

Classify the final change**
In step 6 $\text{C=C}$ gains two $\text{H}$ atoms to become $\text{CH-CH}_{3}$. Gain of hydrogen is reduction. It can also be correctly called hydrogenation or electrophilic addition of hydrogen.

Final answer: step 1: electrophilic substitution (electrophilic aromatic substitution / Friedel-Crafts alkylation)
step 6: reduction (hydrogenation / addition)
